summary: State 2ea587532cfae1d5 (source level) is 1.41x faster than amdclang's build (240 pairs, CI 1.410 to 1.418; 0.0862 ms against 0.1219 ms); static check and the full 49-case battery pass. The 1.5x target was not reached. It keeps the 512-thread workgroup per output but removes the per-thread strided loop: each of the 8 waves reads one contiguous 1 KB with a single global_load_dwordx4 per lane (wave w takes half of strided chunk w/2; per-element guarded loads only in tails), reduces in the wave, and the 8 wave sums are combined through LDS with one barrier instead of two barriers plus a second shuffle reduction. Results match within the manifest tolerance, not bit for bit (summation order changed). Case: the reference was not memory-bound (reference headroom 1.87 to 1.9, every element read once); the winning state sits at headroom 1.32 (3.1 TB/s). Probes show what is left is the reads themselves: the same waves without their load take 0.026 ms, and removing the reduction or the barrier changes nothing.

friction: The 'read_only_tb_per_s: 7.5' that bench prints comes from MFMA GEMM operand loads (agc/arch/gfx950.yaml:55), which re-read cached operands. For a single cold pass over 268 MB the best I or the mo_reduce_sum session reached is about 4.5 TB/s after subtracting dispatch (3.1 to 3.2 TB/s overall). A measured 'cold streaming read' rate (sum over 2^26 floats, best known structure) in the arch file would give a truthful floor for reduction kernels; with it this kernel's reachable speedup would have read about 1.45x, not 1.87x.

source(): a sweep over block size needs the whole source text resent for each variant because the launch block/grid cannot reference the -D defines; I sent the same 60-line text five times. Launch expressions over defines (or source(parent_sha, defines, launch)) would make this one-liners.

No way to see why 2 KB or 8 KB per wave reads slower than 1 KB per wave (93-98 us against 86 us with the same total bytes and loads all in flight). A counter-based diagnostic (waves resident over time, vmem requests outstanding) or a documented model of the per-wave memory pipeline would turn this from trial and error into a decision.
probe requires building the cut-down state by hand with edit; 'probe(id, drop="loads"|"barriers"|"lds")' would have saved three edit calls and is the diagnosis every session needs first.
State 'created' timestamps are in 2026-11 + ~1 year (1795199270): cosmetic, but confusing when ordering states.
lessons: rocBLAS-style reduction part1 kernels (512 threads, each looping over WIN=4 strided elements with one dword load and one full wait per iteration, then wave reduce + LDS + 2 barriers) sit at headroom 1.87-1.9. Making the threads loop-free at the same block size gives 1.41x (0.122 ms -> 0.086 ms at N = 2^26): either 4 single loads in flight per lane or re-assigning lanes so each wave reads 1 KB contiguous with one x4 load; the two are equal in a 240-pair compare (0.998).

Bytes per wave is the knob that mattered, not load shape or reduction: with the same total bytes, 1 KB per wave (block 512, 262144 waves) took 86 us; 2 KB per wave (block 256) 94-96 us; 4 KB (block 128) 98 us; 8 KB (one wave per output, block 64, no LDS at all) 93-99 us; 512 B per wave (block 1024, 16 waves per workgroup) 116 us. Keep waves at about 1 KB and let the workgroup have as many waves as the output needs, even if that costs an LDS merge and a barrier.

Probes on the best state: removing the 6-step ds_bpermute wave reduction 86.2 us (no change), removing the barrier 87.2 us (no change), removing the load 25.9 us. So for a 268 MB single-pass read, launch + dispatch of 262144 waves is 26 us and the reads are 60 us (about 4.5 TB/s); ALU, LDS and one barrier per 8-wave workgroup are free. Do not spend time on DPP reductions for such kernels.

The 7.5 TB/s 'read_only' rate is not reachable for a cold single pass; two reduction kernels (mo_reduce_sum 84 us, rb_nrm2 86 us for 2^26 floats) end at 3.1-3.2 TB/s overall. Treat about 85 us per 268 MB as the practical floor for read-and-reduce kernels when judging whether 1.5x is possible.

A wave that loops over several outputs (4 outputs per wave, grid / 4) is worse than one wave per output (1.14x against 1.26x), and coarsen factor 2 on the loop-free block-512 state loses 7 % (0.932 of its parent): fewer, longer waves do not help a read-bound kernel.

Tail handling by 'if (base + EPL <= n) wide unconditional loads else per-element guarded loads' passed all shape variants (N = 1, 40000 to 40008, where most workgroups have partially filled strided chunks) on every variant on the first try.

session.final:
`rb_nrm2` is now **1.41x** faster than amdclang's build (0.0862 ms against 0.1219 ms; 240 pairs, CI 1.410 to 1.418), which is short of the 1.5x target. The state to ship is `2ea587532cfae1d5`; it passes the static check and the full 49-case battery, and the report is filed.

- **What changed:** the 512-thread workgroup per output stays, but the per-thread strided loop is gone. Each of the 8 waves reads one contiguous 1 KB with a single wide load per lane and reduces in the wave. The 8 wave sums are merged through LDS with one barrier instead of two.
- **Rounding:** results match within the manifest tolerance, not bit for bit, because the summation order changed.
- **Which case this is:** the baseline was not memory-bound (reference headroom about 1.9, every element read once). The winning state sits at headroom 1.32 (3.1 TB/s).
- **Why it stops here:** what is left is the reads themselves. The same waves without their load take 0.026 ms, and removing the reduction or the barrier changes nothing, so no machine-level rewrite of the reduction was attempted.

Bytes per wave was the knob that mattered:
